context: Al-Falaq came down paired with An-Nas, and the Prophet ﷺ announced them with wonder: do you not see verses revealed this night the like of which has never been seen? Qul a’udhu bi-rabbil-falaq and Qul a’udhu bi-rabbin-nas. The account is in Muslim from Uqbah ibn Amir. The scholars differ whether the pair is Makkan or Madinan; many tafsirs connect them to the sound Bukhari account of the spell cast on the Prophet ﷺ by Labid ibn al-A’sam, though the link of their revelation to that event is a later addition, and honesty keeps the two reports distinct.

What is beyond dispute is how he ﷺ used them. Aishah relates that every night he would cup his palms, recite Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, and An-Nas into them, and wipe over his body, and in his final illness she did it for him with his own hands. He taught them as the morning and evening shield, and said that nothing compares to them for the one seeking refuge. With these surahs the community learned that fear has a liturgy: darkness, sorcery, and envy are real, and the answer to all three is a Lord who splits the dark with dawn.
name_story: The surah is named for al-falaq, the daybreak, the splitting-open: the Lord who cracks the night with dawn, the seed with the shoot, and every siege with rescue. With An-Nas it forms al-mu’awwidhatan, the two surahs of seeking refuge, a title given by the Prophet ﷺ himself.

movements.h: Refuge with the Splitter of dawn
movements.note: The command is to say it aloud: I take refuge with the Lord of the daybreak from the evil of what He created, all harm at once placed under the authority of its own Maker.
Then the fears are named one by one and shrunk by naming: the settling night, the blowers on knots practicing sorcery, and the envier when he envies.

themes.d: Isti’adhah, taking refuge, is said, not merely felt: qul, say it, the soul physically running to its Lord the way a child runs behind a father.
From the evil of what He created: harm has no independent throne; it exists inside His dominion, which is exactly why refuge with Him works.
Night, sorcery, envy: the surah drags the vague dreads of the heart into the light and lists them, and a named fear is already half-disarmed.
Idha hasad, when he envies: the eye’s harm activates when envy acts, so the surah teaches both refuge from enviers and vigilance against becoming one.

heart: Al-Falaq recited slowly is the believer’s answer to the dark, and its first word of address is already the cure: not Lord of the night, but Lord of the daybreak. The surah makes you seek shelter from darkness with the One whose signature is splitting it, so hope is built into the grammar before any fear is named. Then the three darknesses file past, the night that hides things, the malice that works unseen, the envy that smiles to your face, and the reciter realizes the surah has covered every direction harm arrives from: circumstance, enemy craft, and the resentful heart nearby.

Whoever makes this surah a nightly habit, palms cupped as the Prophet ﷺ taught, discovers its quiet psychological gift: fear is no longer managed alone. The dark is still dark, but it has an owner, and you know Him, and the last thing your body feels before sleep is His name wiped over it.

passages.why: The address that carries the cure: refuge from darkness sought with the Lord of the daybreak.
The last named fear, envy, the harm that arrives through a smiling face, placed under His protection.

connections.why: An-Nas is its inseparable twin: Al-Falaq shelters from harms outside the chest, An-Nas from the whisper inside it.
Al-Ikhlas states the creed and the two refuges guard it: the Prophet ﷺ recited the three together each night over his palms.

virtue.text: The Prophet ﷺ said of Al-Falaq and An-Nas: verses revealed this night the like of which has never been seen, and he made them his nightly and morning refuge, reciting them over his palms and wiping his body.
